It's a truly impressive natural spectacle – and one you can experience up close: the trail follows the course of the Krimml Waterfalls and links several viewpoints. From the first panoramic spot to the top, the water is constantly changing shape. Each section of the trail reveals a different interplay between water and rock.
The Krimml Waterfalls in the Hohe Tauern National Park are the highest waterfalls in Europe. At times, the water rushes down the rock in narrow streams. At others, it fans out or briefly disappears between the rock layers before reappearing with full force. Information boards along the trail explain how the waterfalls were formed, the geological features of the landscape and the flora and fauna of the Hohe Tauern National Park.
The Krimml WaterWorlds offer an interactive experience centred around the element of water, located right next to the Krimml Waterfalls.
In the winter months, the waterfalls are illuminated until 9.30 pm, with a romantic torchlight walk and a drink.
At 2.6 miles, the waterfall trail winds its way up in switchbacks alongside the Krimml Waterfalls, linking viewpoints across the three cascades.
A leisurely ride along great rivers, cultural highlights and culinary discoveries: the Tauern Cycle Path through the Alps never fails to impress.
The Krimml Waterfalls are situated in the village of Krimml in the Hohe Tauern National Park in SalzburgerLand.
The Krimml Waterfalls are reachable by car as well as by public transport from Zell am See. For the last mile, there is a bus or the local Pinzgau train - depending on the season.
The Krimml Waterfall Trail is open every day from 1st May until the end of October (admission fee applies).
The barrier-free path leads from the car parks to the lowest waterfall, including wheelchair-accessible toilets.
Trail user fee and combined ticket Krimml WaterWorlds and Waterfall Trail.
Hohe Tauern Health combines multi-day stays in Krimml with a structured therapy programme. Designed for people with allergies, asthma or COPD, it brings together time at the therapy site by the Krimml Waterfalls with breathing exercises, movement sessions, talks and personal support from trained specialists.
Depending on the programme, consultations and functional assessments may also be included. Partner properties in Krimml offer accommodation tailored to the programme, so therapy and stay can be combined seamlessly. Programmes run on fixed dates and vary in length and scope. Preparatory information, details of the programme structure and participation requirements are available on request.
Allow around three hours for a visit. The lowest waterfall is around 10 to 15 minutes from the car park, and the ascent to the uppermost waterfall takes approximately one hour and 15 minutes.

The Krimml Waterfall Path is open continuously from 1 May to the end of October (entry fee applies). The falls are at their most powerful in early summer, when snowmelt and rainfall increase the volume of water.
Yes. The path to the lower waterfall is easily manageable with children. Those continuing to the uppermost waterfall should be reasonably fit and sure-footed. The Krimmler WasserWelten at the entrance to the waterfall path uses interactive stations to share fascinating facts about water.

The Krimml Waterfalls ( German : Krimmler Wasserfälle ), with a total height of 380 metres (1,247 feet), are the highest waterfall in Austria . [ 1 ] The falls are on the Krimmler Ache river and are located near the village of Krimml in the High Tauern National Park in Salzburg state.
Krimmler Waterfalls is a tiered waterfall .  The waterfall begins at the top of the Krimmler Ache valley, and plunges downward in three stages. The upper stage has a drop of 140 metres (460 ft) , the middle of 100 metres (330 ft) , and the lowest a drop of 140 metres (460 ft) . The highest point of the waterfall is 1,470 metres (4,823 ft) above sea level. [ 2 ]
The Krimmler Ache is a glacial stream whose flow varies greatly with season. Its volumetric flow in June and July is 5.6 cubic metres per second (1,500 USgal/s) , while in February it is only 0.14 cubic metres per second (37 USgal/s) . The greatest measured flow was on 25 August 1987, when it was 166.7 cubic metres per second (44,000 USgal/s) .
After the falls, the river joins the Salzach , which flows to the Inn , then into the River Danube and finally to the Black Sea .
To ensure that tourists could see more of the waterfall without difficulty, Ignaz von Kürsinger, from Mittersill , created a path to the upper part of the waterfall. In 1879, the Austrian Alpine Club improved the road to provide a more panoramic view. About 400,000 people visit the falls annually. The misty spray of the waterfall creates ideal growth condition for hundreds of mosses, lichens and ferns. The surroundings are the habitat for 62 bird species. [ 3 ]
There is a negative impact on the local residents due to the high traffic level in a small village, and because of erosion to the road. [ citation needed ]
